title: Insert Interval
description:
# Insert Interval

You are given an array of non-overlapping closed intervals `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [starti, endi]`. The intervals are sorted in ascending order by `starti`. You are also given one closed interval `newInterval = [start, end]`.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` and return the new sorted list of non-overlapping intervals. If the new interval overlaps one or more existing intervals, merge all of them into a single interval.

Two intervals overlap when they share at least one point. For example, `[1,5]` and `[5,7]` overlap and merge into `[1,7]`, but `[1,5]` and `[6,8]` remain separate.

Return the intervals after the insertion.

## Example 1:

**Input:** intervals = [[1,3],[6,9]], newInterval = [2,5]
**Output:** [[1,5],[6,9]]
**Explanation:** `[2,5]` overlaps `[1,3]`, so those two ranges become `[1,5]`. `[6,9]` stays separate.

## Example 2:

**Input:** intervals = [[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]], newInterval = [4,8]
**Output:** [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]]
**Explanation:** The new interval overlaps `[3,5]`, `[6,7]`, and `[8,10]`, so those three ranges and the new interval merge into `[3,10]`.

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= intervals.length <= 10^4`
*   `intervals[i].length == 2`
*   `0 <= starti <= endi <= 10^5`
*   `intervals` is sorted by `starti` in ascending order.
*   `intervals` contains no overlapping intervals before insertion.
*   `newInterval.length == 2`
*   `0 <= start <= end <= 10^5`

solutions.name: Three-Phase Linear Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the sorted, disjoint input directly. First copy every interval that ends before the new interval starts. Then keep expanding a local `[start, end]` while intervals overlap it. Finally append the merged interval and copy every interval that starts after it.

## Key Insight

Because the original intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, all intervals affected by the insertion form one contiguous block. Once an interval starts after the current merged end, no later interval can overlap either.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because each interval is inspected once.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the returned interval array may contain all original intervals plus the new one.

solutions.name: Binary Search First Affected Interval
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use binary search on interval ends to find the first interval that could overlap `newInterval`, and binary search on interval starts to find the last interval that could overlap it. Copy the untouched prefix, merge only that candidate block, and copy the untouched suffix.

## Key Insight

The sorted order lets us locate the overlap window by boundary comparisons: intervals with `end < start` are definitely left of the new interval, while intervals with `start > end` are definitely right of it.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n). The searches cost O(log n), but building the returned array is linear.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the answer array is newly allocated.

solutions.name: Append Then Sort And Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Ignore the special insertion structure and solve the more general merge-intervals problem. Append the new interval, sort every interval by start, and run the standard merge pass over the sorted list.

## Key Insight

This is slower than the linear solution, but it is a useful correctness baseline: if the sorted input guarantee were removed, this route would still be valid after sorting.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), dominated by sorting the `n + 1` intervals.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the combined list and result are stored.

solutions.name: TreeMap Ordered Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert all ranges into a `TreeMap` keyed by start, including the new interval. Iterate the ordered map and merge each entry into the current output tail when it overlaps that tail.

## Key Insight

An ordered map is a data-structure version of the general merge idea. It makes the ordering operation explicit and is useful when intervals arrive through incremental insertions instead of a plain array.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), because each interval is inserted into the ordered map.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because the map and output store the intervals.

solutions.name: Endpoint Event Sweep
solutions.description:
## Approach

Convert every interval into two endpoint events: one start event and one end event. Sweep coordinates in sorted order, increasing the active count for starts before decreasing it for ends at the same coordinate. Open an output interval when coverage rises from zero and close it when coverage falls back to zero.

## Key Insight

Processing starts before ends at the same coordinate preserves closed-interval overlap: `[1,5]` and `[5,7]` stay connected. Separate coordinates with a real gap, such as `[1,5]` and `[6,8]`, close and reopen as different intervals.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n), because the event coordinates are stored in a sorted map.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because every interval contributes endpoint events.
